summary: This program stores three Book objects in an ArrayList and then exercises the everyday List operations: counting items, fetching one by position, adding a duplicate, removing an item, testing for membership, and asking whether the list is empty.

lines.text: ArrayList is the resizable list implementation that actually holds the books, and it must be imported before it can be used.
List is the interface that describes what any list can do, which is what the variable will be declared as.
The variable's type is the general List interface while the object created is a concrete ArrayList; the <Book> part promises the list will only ever hold Book objects.

lines.code: Book sherlock = new Book("The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes", "Arthur Conan Doyle", "Mystery");
lines.text: Each book is created once and kept in its own variable, so the same object can later be added, removed, or searched for by name.
add appends an object to the end of the list, so the list grows as books arrive rather than needing a fixed size up front.
The enhanced for loop walks through every element of the list in order without you having to manage an index counter.
size reports how many elements the list currently holds; the \n prints a blank line first to separate the sections of output.
get retrieves an element by position, and list positions start at 0, so index 0 is the first book added.
A List permits duplicates, so adding the same object a second time makes the size grow to four and The Hobbit appear twice.
remove deletes only the first matching element, which is why one copy of The Hobbit is still in the list afterwards.
contains searches the list for a matching element and answers with true or false, saving you from writing a loop to look for it.
isEmpty is the readable way to ask whether the list has no elements; here it reports false because books remain.
